body: Is there a reason why these aren't exposed to the script bindings?

Nitpick, but I personally feel like this should be named either `FuzzySearchMatch` or `FuzzySearchResult`, so as to "namespace" the type a bit. Obviously the latter would collide with the native type, but only having the `RefCounted` type resolves that problem.

I would maybe argue that should be done for `FuzzyTokenMatch` as well, but since it's purely internal it's less relevant I guess, so might be better suited for a separate PR (if at all).
These are exposed (and bound) as `float`, but the actual underlying variable is `int`, which leads to weird truncation. I assume that's not the intention?

I'm mostly thinking out loud here, but I can't help but wonder if it makes sense to expose this as well perhaps. What constitutes a word boundary tends to be somewhat contentious and sometimes domain-specific.

Thoughts?

body:
I'd suggest leaving out the "efficient" part. It's arguably subjective, and not really relevant to the API.

```suggestion
		Provides fuzzy string searching and matching capabilities.
```

I realize this is not a new thing in this PR, but I do question the usefulness of being able to set the query separately like this. Is there a good reason why that's the case? I would normally expect to pass it in along with the candidates in `search` and `search_all`.

I'd recommend against doing this kind of casting. If you absolutely have to then you should at least use a `const_cast` so it's clear what's happening, but the more proper fix is to either:

1. Make `tokens` and `dirty_tokens` (and whatever else is needed) into `mutable` variables, so they can be mutated from `const` methods, which can be seen in several places throughout the engine.
2. Just drop `const` from `search` and `search_all`.

Unless you feel that option 2 would severely hinder certain use-cases then I'd just go for that.
Is this `TODO` here still relevant after exposing the parameters?

No, this is just crust from an earlier version of the code. I don't think anything ever benefited from having the query tokens cached and it definitely did cause some bugs; passing along the query in the public methods here and then passing the tokens to a new private score helper cleans most of this up.

It's been a while since I made this PR but I think I skipped it because of how particular it is to the current implementation and I didn't think it made sense to bake it into the public api. But if it's useful internally it could be useful externally and the api can just be marked experimental as well.

I think that could be a good addition. In general I'm not sure how many knobs should be exposed for tuning scoring for a particular use case vs the current one-size-fits-all approach. Like should the path-specific rightmost-`'/'` handling in the scoring be configurable? Should the scoring weights be configurable? Since the boundary characters specifically affect a single tie-breaker check I'm not sure domains with other relevant boundary characters would really see matching degrade much with the current code.

I guess not. It's kinda like the callout in `_score_token_match` "This can always be tweaked more" but if scoring is perfect than any use case should be able to set reasonable values for the albeit totally naive `cull_score` computation. I think I left the todo because I wasn't sure how well that computation would work.

The only other spot I think this could help is to reserve the token match vector since we always match against all tokens, even if a particular token match is empty and relies on miss_budget being large enough. I'll setup a benchmark to verify but it makes sense that it would improve perf.

Yeah, all good questions that I don't really have a good answer to.

The usual mantra in Godot is to not expose anything until enough people ask for it, so in that sense we might want to hold off with exposing things like `boundary_chars`, and maybe even things like `filter_cutoff` and `filter_factor`.

But I can't help but feel like it would just be a matter of time before people find `max_misses` to be too blunt of an instrument to tune `FuzzySearch` with, so in that sense it might be justified to expose as many knobs as possible. It's hard to know where to draw the line though.

I guess another question worth asking is whether we think exposing all these knobs sets us up for problems in the future. If we were to expose more than one fuzzy algorithm (as an `algorithm` property or something), would it then be problematic to have a bunch of parameters that only suit one of them? I'm not sure.

A couple of `FuzzySearchMatchData` members are seemingly not being cleared in this path, like `token_matches`, `match_interval` and `score`, making reuse of `r_result` problematic. I assume that's not intended?
Why is it that this takes forward slash into account but not backslash, seeing as how backslash is considered a boundary character?

Would it make sense to enforce this range from the code as well (with an `ERR_FAIL_*` or something) rather than just hoping people read the documentation?

The same goes for `filter_cutoff` I guess, and maybe some of the other ones as well.

Nitpick, but this looks like it can be `const`.
```suggestion
TypedArray<Vector2i> FuzzySearchMatch::get_matched_substrings() const {
```

Assuming we don't make this configurable, this either needs to be made `static` (to ensure internal linkage) or we rewrite `_is_boundary_char` to just be a simple `switch` with UTF-32 cases, i.e.:

```cpp
switch (p_char) {
    case U'/':
    case U'\\':
    case U'-':
    case U'_':
    case U'.':
    case U' ':
        return true;
    default:
        return false;
}
```

This needs `static`.

```suggestion
static void remove_low_scores(Vector<FuzzySearchMatchData> &p_results, float p_cull_score) {
```

This was because godot standardizes paths to use forward slash ([docs](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/io/data_paths.html#path-separators)):
> To make supporting multiple platforms easier, Godot uses UNIX-style path separators (forward slash /). These work on all platforms, including Windows.

Although yeah with that in mind I'm not sure how often backslash would match as a boundary character. I did test the old PR on windows as well but maybe it's worth double checking the behavior.

That's interesting, I'm not experienced with c/c++ and never thought about that for const. It looks like c++11 changed (or clarified?) const to imply internal linkage but static const is more common in the codebase anyways.
